title: The clock is a budget (part 3 of 3)
outcomes: Reads a time control such as 10+5 and works out total time and average time per move
Plans a reserve and a per-move average
Tells forced, equal-choice and tempting-move positions apart
Writes a time plan before a game and compares it afterwards

steps.text: Part 3 of 3: The clock is a budget. This part covers Check yourself. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

steps.prompt: Explain to a friend why a forced move should cost almost no clock, and what you do with the seconds you saved. Write two sentences in your own words, then tick what you included.

fields.label: A forced move leaves nothing to decide
The saved seconds go to positions that need a decision

steps.text:
A model answer: when the rules leave one move, thinking cannot improve it, so play it. The seconds saved are a gift to later moves.
[I] Engine-equal does not mean unimportant: choosing a plan in a balanced position is a human decision, so spend saved seconds there. A tempting capture also deserves a count of the guards.

**A routine for any move.** Ask in order: (1) How many legal moves do I have? If one, play it. (2) Is there a check, capture or threat for either side? Count guards and values. (3) If not, pick a plan, choose a sensible move and go.
[I] A habit to practise, not a law. [H] When low on clock, shorten step 3 and choose the simplest safe move; one quick blunder may cost more than many slightly inferior moves. Check it against your lost games.

steps.prompt: Write a time plan for your next game before you start. After the game, compare the plan with what really happened; the gap is the information.

fields.label: Average seconds per move that leaves:
After the game: which kind of position took most of my time?

steps.text: **Remember.** Spend the clock where it matters. If the rules leave one legal move, play it at once and keep the seconds. If there is a check, capture or threat, count guards and values. If not, pick a sensible plan and go. When low on clock, shorten that last step and choose the simplest safe move.
